Full dataset: linear projections (PCA and ICA) · variant textonly

A one-off companion to the book-only PCA/ICA report, now for all 2,910 chunks: 956 from articles, 976 from the books, 978 from videos, each embedded from its own text only. PCA and ICA are linear: every axis is one fixed direction in the 1,024-dimensional embedding space, so the axes can be read. Unlike the books, most chunks have no chapter, so each axis is described by the chunks at its ends, the video tags and book chapters that are over-represented there, and how much of it is explained by the source.

What was done

  1. Centring. The average vector of all chunks was subtracted (no per-source correction: the source effect is part of what this report measures).
  2. PCA finds the directions of largest variation, in order (PC1 the largest).
  3. ICA (FastICA, 20 components) finds directions whose scores are as independent and long-tailed as possible; each tends to pick out one theme or one kind of text. Signs were set so the long tail is positive.
  4. Describing an axis. For the 30 chunks scoring highest (and for PCA also lowest): their mix of sources, the video tags most over-represented among them compared with all videos (shown if at least 3 of the videos carry the tag), the book chapters they come from, and the first titles.
  5. Source effect. η² (eta squared) = share of an axis' variance explained by the source alone, from 0 (none) to 1 (the axis only tells articles, books and videos apart).

PCA: how much does each direction explain?

Reading it: PC1 explains 6.3%, PC2 3.6%; the first 20 components explain 33%, and 52 are needed for half. PC1 is 1.7 times as large as PC2, and the table below shows that it is partly the kind of text: the source alone explains 36% of its variance.

Cumulative variance:

Reading it: the share of all differences between chunks explained by the first k principal components together (out of 1024 components in total). Two components, the most a flat PCA map can show, explain 10%. Half needs 52 components, 80% 175, 90% 270 and 95% 357. The curve rises gradually: no small set of directions captures most of the content.

Reading it: PC1 has a source η² of 0.36: on average it separates book prose (low end) from video descriptions (high end); average PC1 scores: articles -0.01, books -0.13, videos +0.14. This is the source clustering found in the UMAP reports, appearing as the linear direction with the largest source effect. The further components have small source η² (at most 0.13 for PC2–PC6) and are mostly topical: the texts at their two ends show the subjects they contrast.

Reading it: 8 components are themes whose top chunks come from more than one source: IC1: Startovač, Anarchoagorism book campaign; IC2: Bitcoin, cryptocurrencies; IC3: Austrian school of economics; IC4: education system; IC5: 15. Law enforcement; IC6: alcohol, drug legalisation; IC7: economics, Austrian school of economics; IC8: respect, self-management. They are the linear counterpart of the topic regions on the maps, and they connect the same subject across sources. 12 components are dominated by a single source: IC9: Urza and Tim want Bitcoin, not Czech Koruna (videos); IC10: 2020 Holiday Mode Off (articles); IC11: Story three (books); IC12: Children from Ježek, Gabriel and Urza with lo (articles); IC13: Urza in deCentral: Freedom (speech) (articles); IC14: Lecture for SŠINFIS in Pilsen (videos); IC15: Cryptocurrency (books); IC16: Hell is going through the city! (articles); IC17: When the state (antimonopoly authority) does (books); IC18: Anarcho-capitalism on the front lines: Fireme (books); IC19: Freeport Studio: Freeport House with Michal K (videos); IC20: 21. The future (books). The 7 drawn from articles or videos are mostly recurring formats or series (yearly notices, article series, video series, panel discussions) whose texts are alike because of their template. The 5 drawn from the books are book chapters or parts (in subject or style) with no close counterpart elsewhere. Some single-source components are subjects that only one source covers in depth (check their top texts): that is itself a coverage finding, not a defect.

Conclusions

  • The strongest linear direction is partly the kind of text. PC1 separates book prose from video descriptions (source η² 0.36), confirming in linear form what the UMAP reports found: the kind of text is a substantial part of the embedding.
  • Beneath it, the directions are topical. From PC2 on (source η² at most 0.13 up to PC6), and in 17 of 20 ICA components (η² below 0.10), the source explains little; the axes are subjects.
  • ICA separates themes from single-source components. 8 of 20 components are cross-source themes, 12 are dominated by one source (formats, series, or chapters of the books). The theme components show where Urza addresses the same idea in more than one source; the single-source ones point to template texts (notices, series intros) that a coverage measure may want to discount, or to subjects only one source covers.
  • For the coverage map: scoring a political question along the theme components would show which of Urza's themes it touches; the format components are a tool for spotting boilerplate. As in the book report, components depend on the number chosen and the random start: a lens, not a fixed taxonomy.
